name: Giant Pacific Octopus
habitat: Rocky reefs and kelp forests of the North Pacific
funFact: Can change color and texture in milliseconds to blend with surroundings.
description: The giant Pacific octopus is the largest known octopus species, renowned for its intelligence and ability to solve puzzles. It has three hearts, blue blood, and eight dexterous arms lined with suckers.

name: Common Octopus
habitat: Coral reefs and rocky shores of tropical and temperate waters
funFact: Can squeeze through any opening larger than its beak.
description: The common octopus is a highly intelligent marine invertebrate with excellent eyesight and problem-solving abilities. It uses ink clouds and camouflage as primary defense mechanisms.

name: Blue-Ringed Octopus
habitat: Shallow coral reefs and tide pools of the Pacific and Indian Oceans
funFact: Its venom contains tetrodotoxin, potent enough to kill 26 humans.
description: The blue-ringed octopus is a small but deadly cephalopod native to coral reefs. Despite its diminutive size, its bright blue rings serve as a warning of its highly potent venom.

name: Mimic Octopus
habitat: Shallow muddy flats and river mouths of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Can impersonate over 15 different species including lionfish and sea snakes.
description: The mimic octopus is a master of disguise, capable of altering its shape, color, and behavior to resemble other marine animals. It was only discovered in 1998 off the coast of Indonesia.

name: Colossal Squid
habitat: Deep waters of the Southern Ocean
funFact: Has the largest eyes of any animal, up to 10 inches in diameter.
description: The colossal squid is one of the largest invertebrates on Earth, inhabiting the frigid deep waters of the Antarctic. Its massive eyes are adapted to detect light in the perpetual darkness of the deep sea.

name: Humboldt Squid
habitat: Deep waters of the eastern Pacific Ocean
funFact: Also called the jumbo squid or red devil for its aggressive nature.
description: The Humboldt squid is a large, aggressive cephalopod named after the Humboldt Current. It hunts in packs and is known for its rapid growth rate and voracious appetite.

name: Giant Squid
habitat: Deep waters of the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans
funFact: Was considered a mythical creature until first photographed alive in 2004.
description: The giant squid is one of the most mysterious creatures of the deep ocean. With eyes the size of dinner plates and tentacles reaching over 40 feet, it is a legendary predator of the abyss.

name: Firefly Squid
habitat: Coastal waters of the western Pacific Ocean
funFact: Produces its own light through bioluminescent organs called photophores.
description: The firefly squid is a small cephalopod famous for its bioluminescence. Each spring millions gather in Toyama Bay, Japan, creating a spectacular natural light show.

name: Caribbean Reef Octopus
habitat: Shallow coral reefs of the Caribbean Sea
funFact: Has two-thirds of its neurons in its arms rather than its brain.
description: The Caribbean reef octopus is a nocturnal predator that hunts crustaceans and small fish among coral formations. Its chromatophores allow rapid color changes for communication and camouflage.

name: Flamboyant Cuttlefish
habitat: Sandy and muddy bottoms of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: One of only two known poisonous cephalopods.
description: The flamboyant cuttlefish is a small, vibrantly colored cephalopod that walks along the seafloor on its tentacles. It displays pulsating patterns of yellow, maroon, and white as a warning to predators.

name: Common Cuttlefish
habitat: Shallow coastal waters and estuaries of Europe
funFact: Can hypnotize prey with rapidly changing color patterns.
description: The common cuttlefish is a highly intelligent cephalopod with W-shaped pupils and an internal cuttlebone used for buoyancy. It is renowned for its extraordinary ability to change color and texture.

name: Chambered Nautilus
habitat: Deep coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Has remained virtually unchanged for over 500 million years.
description: The chambered nautilus is a cephalopod often called a living fossil, having existed since before the dinosaurs. Its beautiful spiral shell is divided into chambers used for buoyancy control.

name: Argonaut
habitat: Open ocean waters of tropical and subtropical seas
funFact: Females create a paper-thin shell for egg protection, the only octopus to do so.
description: The argonaut, or paper nautilus, is a pelagic octopus where only females produce a delicate calcareous shell. Males are much smaller and lack shells entirely.

name: Vampire Squid
habitat: Oxygen minimum zones of the deep sea
funFact: Is neither a true squid nor a true octopus but occupies its own order.
description: The vampire squid inhabits the deep ocean's oxygen minimum zones. Despite its name, it feeds on marine snow rather than prey, and can turn itself inside out as a defense mechanism.

name: Strawberry Squid
habitat: Deep waters of the mesopelagic zone worldwide
funFact: Has photophores covering its body that produce a strawberry-red glow to camouflage against predators.
description: The strawberry squid is a deep-sea cephalopod covered in light-producing photophores. Its red coloring is invisible in the deep ocean, providing effective camouflage against predators.

name: Cockatoo Squid
habitat: Deep waters of the North Pacific Ocean
funFact: Inflates its body with seawater to appear larger and more intimidating to predators.
description: The cockatoo squid is a small, translucent deep-sea cephalopod that inflates its body like a balloon when threatened. Its distinctive appearance resembles a cockatoo with its arms raised.

name: Pajama Squid
habitat: Sandy and seagrass habitats of southern Australian waters
funFact: Has a distinctive black-and-white striped pattern resembling striped pajamas.
description: The pajama squid is a small, nocturnal cephalopod with distinctive black and white stripes. It buries itself in sand during the day and emerges at night to hunt small crustaceans.

name: Bobtail Squid
habitat: Shallow coastal waters of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Harbors bioluminescent bacteria in a specialized light organ for counter-illumination camouflage.
description: Bobtail squids are small, round cephalopods that partner with bioluminescent bacteria. The bacteria produce light that matches the moonlight from above, eliminating the squid's shadow.

name: Pygmy Squid
habitat: Seagrass beds of shallow coastal Indo-Pacific waters
funFact: Uses a sticky gland on its nose to attach itself to seagrass blades.
description: The pygmy squid is one of the smallest cephalopods, reaching barely an inch long. It uses a special adhesive gland to attach itself to seagrass blades, waiting to ambush passing prey.

name: American Lobster
habitat: Rocky coastal waters of the western Atlantic
funFact: Can live over 100 years and keep growing throughout its life.
description: The American lobster is a large marine crustacean prized as a delicacy. It uses its powerful claws for defense and crushing prey, and can regenerate lost limbs during molting.

name: European Lobster
habitat: Rocky seabeds of the northeastern Atlantic and Mediterranean
funFact: Can weigh up to 28 pounds and is one of the largest crustaceans in European waters.
description: The European lobster is a large, deep-blue crustacean found along rocky coastlines. It is a solitary nocturnal hunter that preys on fish, crabs, and mollusks.

name: Spiny Lobster
habitat: Coral reefs and rocky crevices of tropical oceans
funFact: Lacks large claws and instead produces loud rasping sounds to deter predators.
description: Spiny lobsters are colorful crustaceans found in tropical marine environments. Unlike true lobsters, they lack large front claws and instead rely on their spiny antennae and a unique alarm call.

name: Slipper Lobster
habitat: Rocky and sandy bottoms of warm temperate seas
funFact: Has distinctive plate-like antennae that resemble slipper soles.
description: Slipper lobsters are robust crustaceans recognized by their flattened, slipper-shaped antennae. They are bottom-dwellers that hunt mollusks and other invertebrates at night.

name: Mantis Shrimp
habitat: Tropical and subtropical shallow waters and burrows
funFact: Can punch with the force of a .22 caliber bullet, breaking aquarium glass.
description: The mantis shrimp is a strikingly colored crustacean with the fastest punch in the animal kingdom. It possesses the most complex eyes known, with 16 types of color receptors compared to humans' three.

name: Peacock Mantis Shrimp
habitat: Tropical coral reefs and sandy burrows of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Can see 16 types of color receptors and perceives ultraviolet and polarized light.
description: The peacock mantis shrimp is one of the most colorful and formidable predators in the reef. Its club-like appendages strike with incredible speed and force, capable of shattering glass aquariums.

name: Spearer Mantis Shrimp
habitat: Mud burrows of tropical Indo-Pacific coastlines
funFact: Has barbed, spear-like appendages for impaling soft-bodied prey like fish.
description: Spearer mantis shrimp are ambush predators that wait at the entrance of their mud burrows. They strike passing prey with barbed, spear-like appendages that can impale fish in milliseconds.

name: Blue Crab
habitat: Coastal waters, estuaries, and bays of the western Atlantic
funFact: Named for its bright blue claws used in mating displays.
description: The blue crab is a commercially important species found along the Atlantic coast of North America. It is an aggressive swimmer and opportunistic feeder that plays a key role in estuarine ecosystems.

name: Red King Crab
habitat: Cold waters of the Bering Sea and North Pacific
funFact: Its spiny shell can span over 5 feet from leg tip to leg tip.
description: The red king crab is one of the largest crabs in the world, prized commercially in Alaska and Russia. Its massive, spiny legs can span over five feet and it can walk up to 100 miles during its annual migration.

name: Japanese Spider Crab
habitat: Deep waters around Japan at 150-800m depth
funFact: Has the largest leg span of any arthropod, up to 12 feet across.
description: The Japanese spider crab holds the record for the largest leg span of any living arthropod. Despite its enormous size, it is a gentle giant that scavenges on the ocean floor.

name: Hermit Crab
habitat: Tropical and subtropical shorelines worldwide
funFact: Must find and upgrade to larger shells as it grows throughout its life.
description: Hermit crabs are decapod crustaceans that use abandoned snail shells to protect their soft abdomens. They are social animals often found in groups, and play dead when threatened.

name: Coconut Crab
habitat: Tropical islands of the Indian and Pacific Oceans
funFact: Has the strongest grip of any animal, strong enough to crack open coconuts.
description: The coconut crab is the largest terrestrial arthropod, capable of cracking coconuts with its powerful claws. Despite its name, it lives primarily on land but must return to the sea to reproduce.

name: Snow Crab
habitat: Cold ocean floors of the North Atlantic and Pacific
funFact: Can tolerate near-freezing water temperatures as low as 0.5 degrees Celsius.
description: The snow crab is a cold-water species that lives on sandy and muddy bottoms. It is an important commercial species in both the Atlantic and Pacific, known for its sweet, tender meat.

name: Fiddler Crab
habitat: Mud flats and salt marshes of tropical and subtropical regions
funFact: Males have one enormous claw they wave to attract mates.
description: Fiddler crabs are small semiterrestrial crabs recognized by the male's single oversized claw used in elaborate mating dances. They are important ecosystem engineers in mangrove and marsh habitats.

name: Mud Crab
habitat: Mangrove swamps and muddy estuaries of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Can grow to 5 pounds and has claws strong enough to sever a human finger.
description: The mud crab is a robust species found in mangrove ecosystems across the Indo-Pacific. It is one of the most commercially important crabs in aquaculture, prized for its sweet, firm meat.

name: Atlantic Ghost Crab
habitat: Sandy beaches of the western Atlantic coast
funFact: Can run up to 10 mph and has stalked eyes that provide 360-degree vision.
description: Ghost crabs are pale, fast-moving crustaceans that burrow in sandy beaches. They are mostly nocturnal and use their large stalked eyes and acute hearing to detect predators and prey.

name: Tropical Hermit Crab
habitat: Tropical tidal zones and coral rubble beaches
funFact: Some individuals live in groups of over 100, sharing shells in a chain.
description: Tropical hermit crabs are colorful land-dwelling crustaceans that inhabit beaches and coastal forests. They are highly social and often form shell exchange chains to ensure all members have appropriate shelter.

name: Coconut Hermit Crab
habitat: Tropical island beaches of the Indian and Pacific Oceans
funFact: Often found in coconut shells and can grow large enough to use coconut husks as shelters.
description: The coconut hermit crab is a large land-dwelling species that inhabits tropical island beaches. It is known for its habit of using coconut shells as mobile homes and feeding on fallen coconuts.

name: Zebra Fiddler Crab
habitat: Mangrove forests and tidal flats of West Africa
funFact: Males wave their oversized claw in a unique rhythm specific to their species.
description: The zebra fiddler crab is named for the distinctive stripes on its carapace. Males perform elaborate claw-waving displays to attract females and defend territory on tropical mudflats.

name: Great Spider Crab
habitat: Muddy and sandy seabeds of the northeastern Atlantic
funFact: Often decorates its shell with sponges and algae for camouflage.
description: The great spider crab is a camouflaged crustacean that attaches organisms to its shell for disguise. It migrates in large numbers to shallow waters for mating each autumn.

name: Portunus Swimming Crab
habitat: Sandy and muddy bottoms of tropical and warm temperate seas
funFact: Has paddle-shaped back legs that allow it to swim rapidly through the water.
description: Swimming crabs are agile crustaceans with modified rear legs that function as paddles. They are aggressive predators that can pursue prey through the water column with remarkable speed.

name: Common Shore Shrimp
habitat: Rocky intertidal zones of the northeastern Atlantic
funFact: Can cling tightly to rocks to survive powerful wave action.
description: Common shore shrimp are small crustaceans inhabiting the turbulent intertidal zone. They use specialized appendages to cling to rocks and forage among algae and barnacles for food.

name: Antarctic Krill
habitat: Open waters of the Southern Ocean
funFact: Forms swarms of billions of individuals visible from space.
description: Antarctic krill are small crustaceans that form the foundation of the Antarctic marine food web. Swarms can contain billions of individuals and are a critical food source for whales, seals, and penguins.

name: Pacific Krill
habitat: Coastal and oceanic waters of the North Pacific
funFact: Is the primary food source for North Pacific right whales.
description: Pacific krill are tiny shrimp-like crustaceans that swarm in massive numbers in the North Pacific. They are essential to the marine food web, feeding on phytoplankton and being consumed by larger marine life.

name: Atlantic Krill
habitat: North Atlantic Ocean from Arctic to subtropics
funFact: Forms dense swarms that can extend for miles and contain trillions of individuals.
description: Atlantic krill are small pelagic crustaceans found throughout the North Atlantic. They are a keystone species, supporting populations of cod, herring, whales, and numerous seabirds.

name: Giant Amphipod
habitat: Deep trenches of the Pacific Ocean
funFact: Can grow up to 20 times larger than typical amphipods.
description: Giant amphipods are deep-sea crustaceans found in ocean trenches up to 10,000 meters deep. Their enormous size compared to shallow-water relatives is an example of deep-sea gigantism.

name: Giant Isopod
habitat: Deep ocean floors of the Atlantic and Pacific
funFact: Can survive up to 5 years without eating by slowing its metabolism.
description: Giant isopods are deep-sea crustaceans that can grow up to 14 inches long. They are scavengers that feed on whale falls and other organic material that sinks to the ocean floor.

name: Moon Jellyfish
habitat: Coastal surface waters of oceans worldwide
funFact: Can reproduce both sexually and asexually, allowing population explosions.
description: Moon jellyfish are one of the most common and widely distributed jellyfish species. Their translucent bells pulse gently through coastal waters, feeding on plankton and small organisms.

name: Lion's Mane Jellyfish
habitat: Cold waters of the North Atlantic and North Pacific
funFact: Tentacles can exceed 120 feet, rivaling the blue whale in length.
description: The lion's mane jellyfish is the largest known jellyfish species. Its mass of long, trailing tentacles resembles a lion's mane and can extend far beyond its bell diameter.

name: Box Jellyfish
habitat: Warm coastal waters of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Has 24 eyes including two that can form images, unlike most jellyfish.
description: Box jellyfish are among the most venomous creatures on Earth. Their nearly transparent, cube-shaped bells and up to 60 tentacles make them difficult to spot in tropical waters.

name: Portuguese Man-of-War
habitat: Surface waters of the Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans
funFact: Is actually a colony of four specialized organisms called zooids, not a single animal.
description: The Portuguese man-of-war is a siphonophore, not a true jellyfish. Its iconic blue float sails on the surface while trailing long, venomous tentacles that can deliver an extremely painful sting.

name: Pacific Sea Nettle
habitat: Coastal waters of the eastern Pacific Ocean
funFact: Its golden-brown bell and long trailing tentacles make it one of the most beautiful jellyfish.
description: The Pacific sea nettle is a large, visually striking jellyfish with a rusty-orange bell and long, coiling tentacles. It feeds on zooplankton, fish eggs, and other jellyfish.

name: Upside-Down Jellyfish
habitat: Shallow mangrove swamps and seagrass beds of tropical waters
funFact: Rests upside-down on the seafloor to expose symbiotic algae to sunlight.
description: The upside-down jellyfish, or Cassiopea, lies bell-down on the substrate to maximize photosynthesis by its symbiotic algae. It pulses gently to circulate water and capture food particles.
region: Tropical Atlantic, Pacific, and Indian Oceans

name: Immortal Jellyfish
habitat: Temperate and tropical waters worldwide
funFact: Can revert from its adult form back to its juvenile polyp stage, effectively reversing aging.
description: The immortal jellyfish, Turritopsis dohrnii, is biologically immortal. When stressed or aging, it reverts to its polyp form and begins its life cycle anew, making it the only known creature capable of true rejuvenation.

name: Sea Wasp
habitat: Coastal waters of northern Australia and Southeast Asia
funFact: Considered the most venomous marine animal, capable of killing a human in minutes.
description: The sea wasp, or Chironex fleckeri, is the largest and most dangerous box jellyfish. Its nearly invisible body and incredibly potent venom make it one of the deadliest creatures in the ocean.
region: Northern Australian and Southeast Asian waters

name: Compass Jellyfish
habitat: Coastal waters of the northeastern Atlantic
funFact: Has distinctive brown V-shaped markings on its bell resembling a compass rose.
description: The compass jellyfish is easily identified by the brown radiating lines on its translucent bell that resemble compass markings. It feeds on small fish and other jellyfish.

name: Fried Egg Jellyfish
habitat: Coastal waters of the northeastern Atlantic and Mediterranean
funFact: Its bell closely resembles a fried egg, with a yellow center surrounded by white.
description: The fried egg jellyfish, or Cotylorhiza tuberculata, is a visually striking species with a bell that looks remarkably like a fried egg. Despite its large size, its sting is relatively mild.

name: Blood Belly Comb Jelly
habitat: Deep waters of the Mediterranean Sea
funFact: Produces brilliant red bioluminescence when disturbed.
description: The blood belly comb jelly is a deep-water ctenophore found in the Mediterranean. When threatened, it produces vivid red bioluminescence, creating a spectacular display in the dark waters.

name: Atolla Jellyfish
habitat: Deep waters of all major oceans
funFact: Produces a pinwheel of bioluminescent light when attacked, known as a burglar alarm.
description: The Atolla jellyfish inhabits the deep ocean and is famous for its burglar alarm display. When attacked, it produces a rotating wheel of blue bioluminescence to attract larger predators that may attack its attacker.

name: Spotted Jelly
habitat: Coastal waters of the western Pacific and Indian Oceans
funFact: Has distinctive brown spots on its translucent bell that give it its name.
description: The spotted jelly is a rhizostome jellyfish with a translucent bell covered in brown spots. It feeds on plankton and small organisms using oral arms lined with tiny mouth openings.

name: Mauve Stinger
habitat: Open ocean waters of the Atlantic and Indo-Pacific
funFact: Can bloom in massive swarms that disrupt fisheries and aquaculture operations.
description: The mauve stinger is a deep-water jellyfish with a distinctive reddish-purple bell covered in nematocyst clusters. It forms massive blooms in open ocean waters.

name: Staghorn Coral
habitat: Shallow tropical coral reefs of the Atlantic and Indo-Pacific
funFact: Can grow up to 8 inches per year, making it one of the fastest-growing corals.
description: Staghorn coral is a critically endangered branching coral species. Once dominant in Caribbean reefs, its populations have declined by over 80% due to disease, bleaching, and predation.

name: Brain Coral
habitat: Tropical coral reefs worldwide
funFact: Can live for nearly a millennium, making it one of the longest-lived organisms on Earth.
description: Brain coral is named for its spherical shape and the winding grooves on its surface that resemble a human brain. It is a slow-growing but extremely long-lived reef-building species.

name: Elkhorn Coral
habitat: Shallow tropical reefs of the Caribbean
funFact: Named for its broad, antler-like branches that resemble elk horns.
description: Elkhorn coral is a critically endangered species that once formed vast reefs throughout the Caribbean. Its large, branching colonies provide essential habitat for hundreds of reef species.

name: Pillar Coral
habitat: Deep reef slopes of the Caribbean
funFact: One of the rarest corals, with no known young produced since 1998 in Florida.
description: Pillar coral is one of the rarest reef-building corals, distinguished by its tall, cylindrical columns that rise from the reef. It is listed as critically endangered with populations plummeting.

name: Fire Coral
habitat: Shallow tropical reefs and rocky substrates worldwide
funFact: Not a true coral but a colony of hydrozoans that delivers a painful sting.
description: Fire coral is a colony-forming hydrozoan that looks like true coral but delivers a painful sting on contact. Its smooth, branching colonies are typically brown, yellow, or reddish in color.

name: Blue Coral
habitat: Reefs of the western Pacific and Indian Oceans
funFact: The only reef-building coral with a blue skeleton, caused by iron salts in its skeleton.
description: Blue coral is a unique reef-building species with a distinctive blue skeleton. It is one of the few corals that can survive in turbid, low-light environments where other corals cannot.

name: Mushroom Coral
habitat: Shallow sandy and rubble areas of Indo-Pacific reefs
funFact: Unlike most corals, mushroom corals are free-living and can move short distances.
description: Mushroom corals are solitary, free-living scleractinian corals shaped like mushrooms. Unlike colonial species, each is a single polyp that can detach and roll across the substrate.

name: Black Coral
habitat: Deep reef walls and seamounts worldwide
funFact: Some colonies have been dated to over 4,000 years old, making them the oldest living organisms on Earth.
description: Black corals are deep-water colonial organisms with a black or dark brown skeleton. They are among the longest-lived organisms on Earth, with some colonies surviving for millennia.

name: Sea Pen
habitat: Soft bottoms of deep ocean floors worldwide
funFact: Is a colony of polyps anchored in sediment, with some species producing bioluminescent waves when disturbed.
description: Sea pens are colonial cnidarians that resemble old-fashioned quill pens. They anchor in soft sediment and can produce bioluminescent waves of light that travel along their colonies.

name: Sea Whip
habitat: Deep reefs and rocky substrates of the Atlantic and Pacific
funFact: Some species produce a compound used in cancer research.
description: Sea whips are octocoral colonies that grow in long, whip-like branches. They are filter feeders that extend polyps into the current to capture plankton and organic particles.

name: Sunflower Sea Star
habitat: Cold, muddy seabeds of the northeastern Pacific
funFact: Can have up to 24 arms and is one of the largest sea stars in the world.
description: The sunflower sea star is one of the largest and fastest sea stars, but populations have crashed by over 90% due to sea star wasting disease. It is now listed as critically endangered.

name: Crown-of-Thorns Starfish
habitat: Coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Can consume up to 10 square feet of coral per year.
description: The crown-of-thorns starfish is a large, multi-armed sea star covered in venomous spines. It is a significant coral predator whose population outbreaks can devastate reef ecosystems.

name: Blue Sea Star
habitat: Shallow sandy flats and seagrass beds of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Its brilliant blue color comes from a pigment that may protect against UV radiation.
description: The blue sea star is a strikingly colored echinoderm that lives on sandy substrates. It feeds on small invertebrates buried in the sand and can regenerate lost arms.

name: Common Starfish
habitat: Rocky shores and tidal pools of the northeastern Atlantic
funFact: Can turn its stomach inside out to digest prey externally.
description: The common starfish is one of the most recognizable sea stars, with five arms and a tough, spiny surface. It feeds on mussels and oysters by everting its stomach through its mouth.

name: Leather Star
habitat: Rocky substrates of the northeastern Pacific
funFact: Has a smooth, leathery texture unlike the rough surface of most sea stars.
description: The leather star is a smooth-skinned sea star found on rocky reefs. It has a distinctive reddish-brown color and a unique garlic-like odor when handled.

name: Common Brittle Star
habitat: Rocky and sandy bottoms of the northeastern Atlantic
funFact: Can detach an arm to escape predators, later regenerating it.
description: Brittle stars are echinoderms with a distinct central disc and five long, slender arms. They are more agile than sea stars, moving by writhing their arms across the seabed.

name: Giant Basket Star
habitat: Deep reefs and rocky walls of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Has thousands of branching arm tips that can entrap plankton and small organisms.
description: The giant basket star is a spectacular echinoderm with a complex network of branching arms. At night, it unfurls its arms into the current to capture plankton and small crustaceans.

name: Feather Star
habitat: Coral reefs and rocky substrates of tropical oceans
funFact: Can swim by rhythmically waving its feathery arms through the water.
description: Feather stars are mobile crinoids that cling to coral or swim through the water column. Their feathery arms filter plankton from passing currents, and they can detach to relocate when conditions change.

name: Crinoid Feather Star
habitat: Deep reefs and coral walls of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Can detach from its substrate and swim to relocate when conditions are unfavorable.
description: Crinoid feather stars are ancient echinoderms related to sea lilies. They perch on coral heads and wave their feathery arms to capture passing plankton from ocean currents.

name: Disk-Brittle Star
habitat: Rocky and sandy bottoms of the northeastern Atlantic
funFact: Can regenerate entire arms and even the central disc if detached.
description: The disk-brittle star is a small, agile echinoderm found in rock crevices and under stones. It is an opportunistic feeder that can regenerate lost body parts rapidly.

name: Purple Sea Urchin
habitat: Rocky intertidal zones of the northeastern Pacific
funFact: Can bore into solid rock using its specialized jaw apparatus called Aristotle's lantern.
description: The purple sea urchin is a spiny echinoderm that inhabits rocky shores. It uses its five-toothed jaw, Aristotle's lantern, to scrape algae and even excavate burrows in solid rock.

name: Long-Spined Sea Urchin
habitat: Tropical coral reefs and rocky substrates worldwide
funFact: Spines can be over a foot long and are mildly venomous.
description: Long-spined sea urchins are tropical echinoderms with extremely long, sharp spines that provide excellent defense. They play a critical role in controlling algal growth on coral reefs.

name: Pencil Urchin
habitat: Rocky reefs and coral rubble of tropical Indo-Pacific
funFact: Has thick, blunt spines that resemble pencils, unlike typical sharp urchin spines.
description: Pencil urchins are named for their thick, cylindrical spines that look like colored pencils. They inhabit tropical reefs where they graze on algae using their complex jaw apparatus.

name: Green Sea Urchin
habitat: Cold rocky shores of the northeastern Atlantic and Pacific
funFact: Can live for over 30 years, making it one of the longest-lived sea urchins.
description: The green sea urchin is a cold-water species found on rocky substrates. It is an important herbivore in kelp forest ecosystems, controlling algal growth and providing food for sea otters.

name: Flower Urchin
habitat: Coral reefs and rocky substrates of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Covered in flower-like structures called pedicellariae that deliver a painful venom.
description: The flower urchin is one of the most dangerous sea urchins, covered in venomous flower-shaped pedicellariae. Despite its beautiful appearance, contact causes intense pain and potential tissue damage.

name: Sand Dollar
habitat: Sandy bottoms of shallow coastal waters worldwide
funFact: The petal-like pattern on its skeleton is actually five sets of tube feet used for breathing.
description: Sand dollars are flat, burrowing sea urchins found on sandy ocean floors. Their flattened bodies and fine spines allow them to bury themselves just beneath the sediment surface.

name: Carpenter Sea Urchin
habitat: Tropical coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Has particularly strong teeth that can bore through solid coral rock.
description: The carpenter sea urchin is named for its ability to excavate burrows in solid coral rock. Its powerful Aristotle's lantern allows it to bore into reef substrates for shelter.

name: Fire Urchin
habitat: Tropical coral reefs of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Has venomous spines that cause intense burning pain, resembling a fire ant sting.
description: The fire urchin is a striking red echinoderm with venomous spines that deliver an intensely painful sting. Despite its danger, it provides a symbiotic home for certain shrimp and crabs.

name: Slate Pencil Urchin
habitat: Rocky reefs of the tropical Indo-Pacific
funFact: Has thick, blunt spines that were historically used as writing instruments.
description: Slate pencil urchins are named for their thick, blunt spines that resemble slate pencils. These colorful echinoderms inhabit tropical reefs where they graze on algae.

name: Tiger Tail Sea Cucumber
habitat: Sandy and muddy substrates of the tropical Indo-Pacific
funFact: Can eject sticky, toxic tubules from its body to entangle predators.
description: The tiger tail sea cucumber is a large, conspicuous species with distinctive dark stripes. It is an important bioturbator, processing sediment and recycling nutrients in tropical marine ecosystems.

name: Lolly Sea Cucumber
habitat: Sandy flats and coral rubble of tropical reefs
funFact: Has a distinctive tube-like body that resembles a lollipop.
description: The lolly sea cucumber is a small, cylindrical species that processes sand and sediment on tropical reefs. It plays a vital role in reef health by recycling organic matter.

name: Pacific Sea Cucumber
habitat: Sandy and muddy bottoms of the northeastern Pacific
funFact: Is commercially harvested as a delicacy in Asian cuisine, known as beche-de-mer.
description: The Pacific sea cucumber is an ecologically important detritivore that processes vast quantities of sediment. It is commercially harvested and considered a culinary delicacy in many Asian cultures.

name: Black Sea Cucumber
habitat: Rocky and sandy substrates of the Indo-Pacific
funFact: Can detach and regrow its internal organs when stressed, a process called evisceration.
description: The black sea cucumber is a large, commercially valuable species found on tropical reefs. It ejects its internal organs as a defense mechanism and later regenerates them completely.

name: Teatfish Sea Cucumber
habitat: Sandy and rubble substrates of tropical Indo-Pacific reefs
funFact: One of the most commercially valuable sea cucumber species, sold as beche-de-mer.
description: The teatfish is a large, highly valued sea cucumber that has been overexploited for the Asian beche-de-mer trade. Its distinctive nipple-like projections give it its common name.

name: Red Sea Cucumber
habitat: Kelp forests and rocky substrates of the northeastern Pacific
funFact: Uses tube feet along its underside to slowly crawl across the seafloor.
description: The red sea cucumber is a common species in Pacific kelp forests. It grazes on detritus and algae on rocky substrates, playing an important role in nutrient cycling.

name: Christmas Tree Worm
habitat: Living coral colonies of tropical Indo-Pacific reefs
funFact: Can retract its colorful spiral plumes into its tube in less than a second.
description: Christmas tree worms are tubeworms that burrow into living coral colonies. Their colorful, spiral-shaped radioles filter plankton from the water and can retract instantly when disturbed.

name: Giant Tube Worm
habitat: Hydrothermal vents of the deep Pacific Ocean
funFact: Has no mouth, stomach, or gut, relying entirely on symbiotic bacteria for nutrition.
description: Giant tube worms are extraordinary deep-sea organisms that thrive at hydrothermal vents. They rely on chemosynthetic bacteria housed in a special organ called the trophosome for all nutrition.

name: Feather Duster Worm
habitat: Coral reefs and rocky substrates of tropical waters
funFact: Its feathery crown of tentacles is used for both feeding and respiration.
description: Feather duster worms are sedentary polychaetes that construct tubes on reef surfaces. Their spectacular crown of feathery tentacles filters plankton and can retract rapidly when threatened.

name: Bearded Fireworm
habitat: Coral reefs and rocky substrates of the tropical Atlantic
funFact: Has hollow, venom-filled bristles that cause intense burning pain on contact.
description: The bearded fireworm is a predatory polychaete with venomous bristles called chaetae. Contact with these white, hair-like structures causes severe pain, inflammation, and numbness.

name: Blue Glaucus
habitat: Surface waters of tropical and temperate oceans
funFact: Floats upside-down on the surface tension of the water, using stored air bubbles.
description: The blue glaucus, or blue dragon, is a tiny, vibrant blue sea slug that floats upside-down on the ocean surface. It stores stinging cells from its prey for its own defense.

name: Spanish Dancer
habitat: Coral reefs of the tropical Indo-Pacific
funFact: Named for its spectacular undulating swimming motion that resembles a flamenco dancer.
description: The Spanish dancer is one of the largest and most colorful nudibranchs. When swimming, it unfurls its brilliant red and white mantle in a mesmerizing undulating display.

name: Leaf Sheep
habitat: Shallow tropical waters of the western Pacific
funFact: Is one of the only animals capable of photosynthesis, stealing chloroplasts from algae.
description: The leaf sheep, or Costasiella kuroshimae, is a tiny sea slug that can photosynthesize like a plant. It steals chloroplasts from the algae it eats and stores them in its body to produce energy.

name: Sea Butterfly
habitat: Open ocean waters from surface to deep sea
funFact: Swims by flapping its wing-like shell extensions, resembling a butterfly in flight.
description: Sea butterflies are tiny marine snails that swim through the open ocean by flapping their wing-like shell extensions. They are an important food source for fish, whales, and seabirds.

name: Sea Angel
habitat: Cold waters of the Arctic, Antarctic, and deep oceans
funFact: Is a shell-less snail that swims with graceful wing-like movements.
description: Sea angels are gelatinous, transparent marine gastropods that lack shells. They swim through cold ocean waters by flapping wing-like appendages and prey on sea butterflies.

name: California Sea Hare
habitat: Rocky intertidal zones and kelp forests of the northeastern Pacific
funFact: Can release a cloud of purple ink when threatened, confusing predators.
description: The California sea hare is a large marine gastropod named for its ear-like rhinophores. It feeds on kelp and seaweed and can release a cloud of purple ink as a defense mechanism.

name: Giant Clam
habitat: Shallow coral reefs of the tropical Indo-Pacific
funFact: Can weigh over 500 pounds and live for more than 100 years.
description: The giant clam is the largest living bivalve mollusk, reaching over four feet in length. Its colorful mantle harbors symbiotic algae that provide much of its nutrition through photosynthesis.

name: Geoduck
habitat: Sandy and muddy bottoms of the northeastern Pacific
funFact: Can live for over 160 years, making it one of the longest-living animals on Earth.
description: The geoduck is the largest burrowing clam in the world, with a siphon that can extend three feet. Native to the Pacific Northwest, it is a prized delicacy in Asian cuisine.

name: Atlantic Surf Clam
habitat: Sandy bottoms of shallow Atlantic waters
funFact: Can propel itself out of the sand using its muscular foot when disturbed.
description: The Atlantic surf clam is a large bivalve found on sandy substrates. It uses its powerful foot to burrow and can explosively eject itself from the sand when threatened by predators.

name: Bay Scallop
habitat: Shallow seagrass beds and sandy bottoms of coastal waters
funFact: Can swim short distances by rapidly clapping its shell valves together.
description: Bay scallops are small, fan-shaped bivalves that live in shallow coastal waters. Unlike most clams, they can swim by rapidly clapping their valves, ejecting water for propulsion.

name: Blue Mussel
habitat: Rocky shores and intertidal zones of the North Atlantic
funFact: Attaches to rocks using strong byssal threads, forming dense beds of thousands.
description: Blue mussels are filter-feeding bivalves that attach to rocks with strong byssal threads. They form dense beds that provide habitat for numerous other species and are commercially cultivated.

name: Thorny Oyster
habitat: Coral reefs and rocky substrates of tropical Indo-Pacific
funFact: Shell is covered in long, sharp spines that deter predators.
description: The thorny oyster is a large, spiny bivalve that cements itself to reef substrates. Its long, sharp spines protect it from predators and can cause painful wounds if touched.

name: Lion Paw Scallop
habitat: Rocky reefs and kelp forests of the northeastern Pacific
funFact: Named for its ridged, colorful shell that resembles a lion's paw.
description: The lion paw scallop is a large, colorful bivalve with a distinctive ridged shell. It can swim by clapping its valves and is found in kelp forests along the Pacific coast.

name: Nautilus Pompilius
habitat: Deep coral reefs of the tropical Indo-Pacific
funFact: Shell follows a logarithmic spiral, one of nature's most perfect mathematical forms.
description: Nautilus pompilius is a cephalopod with a beautiful, spiraled shell that has inspired artists and mathematicians for centuries. It is a living fossil, virtually unchanged for 500 million years.

name: Paper Nautilus
habitat: Open ocean waters of tropical and subtropical seas
funFact: Females create a delicate, paper-thin shell for egg protection.
description: The paper nautilus is an argonaut octopus in which only females produce a fragile, calcareous shell. Males are much smaller and shell-less, using a specialized arm to transfer sperm.

name: Atlantic Horseshoe Crab
habitat: Sandy bottoms and coastal shallows of the western Atlantic
funFact: Has been virtually unchanged for 450 million years, predating the dinosaurs.
description: The Atlantic horseshoe crab is a marine arthropod often called a living fossil. Despite its name, it is more closely related to spiders and scorpions than to true crabs.

name: Japanese Horseshoe Crab
habitat: Sandy and muddy bottoms of coastal Japan and Southeast Asia
funFact: Its blue blood contains Limulus Amebocyte Lysate, used to test for bacterial contamination in medical equipment.
description: The Japanese horseshoe crab is an endangered species whose unique blue blood is vital to modern medicine. The substance in its blood detects bacterial endotoxins in pharmaceuticals and medical devices.

name: Indo-Pacific Horseshoe Crab
habitat: Sandy and muddy bottoms of Southeast Asian coastal waters
funFact: Is the only horseshoe crab species found in Asian coastal waters.
description: The Indo-Pacific horseshoe crab is an endangered marine arthropod found in Southeast Asian coastal waters. Like its Atlantic relative, it has blue blood containing valuable immune cells.

name: Sea Squirt
habitat: Rocky substrates and docks of coastal waters worldwide
funFact: Is more closely related to vertebrates than most invertebrates, being a chordate.
description: Sea squirts are tunicates, marine invertebrates that are surprisingly closely related to vertebrates. As larvae they have a notochord, which they lose as adults when they attach to surfaces and become filter feeders.

name: Marine Flatworm
habitat: Coral reefs and rocky substrates of tropical waters
funFact: Can regenerate an entire organism from a fragment as small as 1/200th of its body.
description: Marine flatworms are colorful, soft-bodied invertebrates that glide across reef surfaces. Despite their simple appearance, they are active predators that can deliver venomous bites.

name: Deep-Sea Pennatula
habitat: Deep muddy bottoms of the Atlantic and Pacific
funFact: Produces bioluminescent waves that travel along its colony when physically disturbed.
description: The deep-sea pennatula is a species of sea pen that inhabits deep muddy bottoms. When disturbed, it produces stunning bioluminescent waves that ripple along its colony.
